chapter_theme: Songs at Tiruvamathur (திருவாமாத்தூர், மாதை): four confessions of bondage to women, seen as deceivers of the young, as Death in a woman's form, as common women singing to the measure of the coin, and as the snare that keeps the poet sunk in caste and clan; he asks for the feet and to stop swinging like a balance beam between devotion and desire.

728.reading: The poet speaks of women whose eyes strike like spears and arrows, whose breasts are like the tusks of a rutting elephant, whose drum-like waists torment young men, and who deceive them boldly, and asks whether, having worshipped and said 'I am your hereditary servant', he must still have his life swing up and down like the beam of a balance in their company. The praise names Murugan who spoke longingly with the hunter girl in the forest and bowed at her feet, the treasure of the ascetics who chant him knowingly as the six-faced lord, at Mathai, the ancient town of those who think of Siva on the bull, where evil deeds run far away.
728.nuance: துலையலை மாறு போல் உயிர் சுழல்வேனோ: the image of a balance beam tipping between his vow of service (வழிவழியான் எனா) and the women is the song's own. அடிதொழுது ஆடும் ஆண்மை: Murugan's bowing at Valli's feet is called manliness.

729.reading: The poet describes women with carp and doe eyes, bamboo shoulders, breasts like lotus buds and elephant tusks and hair darker than collyrium, as if Death had put on a woman's form to seize young men's lives, and asks that he not perish setting his love on the great maya they lay, but be given grace to cherish Murugan's feet even a little. The praise names Murugan the treasure of Siva on the bull, at whose feet Indra, Brahma and Vishnu fall, with Uma on his side and the elephant hide as his cloak, the lord who loves Mathai and whose vel made the demons cry out.
729.nuance: உயர் காலன் பெண் தனக்கு உள கோலாகலம் இன்று எடுத்து: the women are Death himself in a woman's festive dress, come for young men's lives. The plea asks only for கிஞ்சில் அத்தனை, the least amount, of love for the feet. விண்டனக்கு உறவானோன் உடல் கண்படைத்தவன் seems to be Indra, whose body was covered with eyes.

730.reading: The poet speaks of women with dark cloud hair and speech like honey, syrup and fruit, lustful and quick to anger, heavy-breasted, with carp-like eyes, plunderers who sing their love to the measure of the money, common to all, sinners of pleasure, and asks when Murugan will grant grace to him who perishes in their power. The praise is a battle, with drum syllables and ghouls feeding on flesh, and names Murugan son of Uma, the younger sister of Vishnu who bears the discus, and of the lord who wears the serpent, poolai flowers, the moon and arugu grass, at southern Mathai.
730.nuance: பொருள் அளவு ஆசைப்பாடிகள், பொதுவிகள்: love sung to the measure of the coin, and women belonging to all, are the Kural's two charges against the courtesan. Uma as Vishnu's younger sister explains why Vishnu is always Murugan's uncle.

731.reading: The poet speaks of women whose eyes are the arrows of the bodiless Kama, who quarrel and whose minds are set on the coin, frauds with lying speech, in whose flower beds he perishes, and asks to be given the end of the lowness of being sunk in caste and clan, the attainment of the feet high in open space, and much thought of austerity. The praise tells of Krishna, who sleeps on the serpent, plays the flute to the herds, stole butter and curd from the hanging pots and was beaten with the rope, and of Rama who felled the seven trees and Vali and with one arrow the ten heads and twenty arms of Ravana, as uncle, and the six-faced lord of fragrant Mathai.
731.nuance: சாதி குலம் உறு படியினில் முழுகிய தாழ்வு அற: the poet names caste and clan as something he is sunk in and wants freed from, an unusual plea set beside the courtesans. காசின் அளவு ஒருதலை அணு மனதினர் repeats the charge of love measured by the coin. The Krishna scenes (butter, rope) are told unusually fully.

links.note: Both use the courtesan's being common to all as the charge: the Kural's women 'whose goodness belongs to everyone' (பொதுநலத்தார்) and 730's பொதுவிகள். The Kural says the wise don't plunge in; 730 is the confession of one who did.
The Kural's women weigh the profit and then speak of virtue; 731's women have minds set on the coin and lying speech. Both make the calculation the mark of the courtesan.

Tirumular says that for those who hold Nandi in love there is no caste; 731 asks that the lowness of being sunk in caste and clan end when he reaches the feet. Both place caste among what falls away at release.

728 asks whether, though vowed as a hereditary servant, his life must swing like the beam of a balance (துலையலை மாறு போலுயிர் சுழல்வேனோ) between that vow and the women. Kural 118 praises the worthy for being like a balance that levels itself and leans to no side (சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல்). The same instrument is the Kural's figure of steadiness and the song's figure of a soul that cannot settle.

729 says the women are as if Death himself had put on a woman's festive form to seize young men's lives (உயர் காலன் பெண் தனக்கு உள கோலாகலம்). In Kural 1083 the lover says he never knew Death before and now knows it, in a woman's grace and warring eyes (கூற்றென் பதனை இனியறிந்தேன் பெண்டகையால்). The Kural's lover's hyperbole becomes in the song a literal warning, with Death as the one in disguise.

730 calls the women plunderers who sing their love to the measure of the money (பொருளளவு ஆசைப் பாடிகள்) and belong to all. Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, as a lamp's light ends with the oil (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both measure the love exactly by the coin; the Naladiyar adds the image of the lamp going out.
